analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank rule requiring banks to report how they pay executives.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Dodd-Frank, the 2010 financial overhaul, required regulators to write rules making each big financial institution disclose the structure of its incentive-based pay — the bonuses and compensation schemes that can reward excessive risk-taking. H.R. 5998 would have wiped out that reporting requirement entirely, so banks' pay practices would stay off the public record. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, banks and other covered financial institutions would have gained: they would avoid the cost and publicity of disclosing how their bonus and incentive structures work, and avoid outside scrutiny of pay practices that can encourage short-term risk-taking. Institutional investors and consumers would lose the visibility the reporting was designed to provide.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 956 of the Dodd-Frank Act, which requires regulations compelling each covered financial institution to disclose the structures of all incentive-based compensation arrangements it offers [S2] [S3].
Repeal would spare financial institutions the compliance burden of reporting compensation structures and keep those arrangements out of public and regulatory view [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on depositors, investors, and taxpayers, who would remain unable to see the pay structures that reward risk-taking at financial firms — the same kind of compensation practices Congress identified after the 2008 crisis as a contributor to excessive risk. Regulators at the Treasury, Federal Reserve, SEC, FDIC, and other agencies would lose a transparency tool Congress had just given them.

drawbacks.text: Banks would bear real compliance costs under the disclosure rules the bill repeals; reporting every incentive compensation arrangement across all regulated entities is a genuine administrative burden, and the bill's backers could argue the burden is not justified by its benefits [S3].

Transparency about pay structures does not by itself stop risky compensation — firms could still design incentive plans that reward short-term gains; disclosure alone is a modest safeguard, which is an honest limit on what repealing it would change [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits of the bill flow almost entirely to financial institutions, while the cost — losing public visibility into executive pay structures that reward risk — falls on everyone with a stake in the financial system. Given that compensation incentives were a recognized contributor to the 2008 crisis, the transparency requirement was a light-touch response, and repealing it would have removed one of the few low-cost checks on the industry's pay practices. The bill also had no cosponsors, suggesting even within the minority party it drew little support.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee at the end of July 2010 and never came out — no hearing, no vote, nothing before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeb Hensarling introduced the bill on July 30, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].

The complete action history shows no further activity after the referral: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, investors, and regulators are better off, because the Dodd-Frank incentive-compensation disclosure requirement stayed on the books; the banks that would have avoided reporting their pay structures did not get the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and regulators; banks lost the repeal

for.name: Jeb Hensarling
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 30, 2010 to repeal the Dodd-Frank Section 956 compensation-disclosure requirement [S1] [S3] [S5].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill — no hearing or markup was held, and it remained in committee until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the repeal with no cosponsors from either party, and the Democratic-majority committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Banks and other covered financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would have exempted them from disclosing the structure of incentive-based pay arrangements, sparing them compliance costs and public scrutiny of compensation practices that can reward excessive risk-taking. If those pay practices contribute to instability, the public ultimately shares the downside.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (Treasury, Federal Reserve, SEC, FDIC, NCUA, FHFA)
industries.note: Dodd-Frank Section 956 directed these agencies to write the disclosure regulations; repeal would have removed a tool they were using to see and surface risky pay structures across the firms they supervise.
